title: Meclizine and Alcohol: Is It Safe to Drink on Bonine?
excerpt: Can you drink on meclizine (Bonine, Dramamine Less Drowsy, Antivert)? How the two stack up, how long to wait, cruise tips, and the warning signs that need help.
metaDescription: Can you drink on meclizine (Bonine, Antivert)? How meclizine and alcohol interact, how long to wait, cruise tips, and when to get help.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** meclizine (sold as Bonine, Dramamine Less Drowsy, and Antivert) and alcohol both slow down your brain, so taking them together makes you sleepier, dizzier, and less coordinated than either one alone. For a healthy adult, a drink or two on the same day as a single 25 mg dose is unlikely to be dangerous, but the label says to avoid alcohol for a reason. The risk rises with more drinks, with higher doses, with other sedating medicines, and with age. That's why the safest plan is to keep drinking light, never drive, and talk to a pharmacist if anything else is in the mix.

**The quick rules:** Expect meclizine to last the whole day you take it. Keep alcohol to one or two drinks at most if you've taken it. Never drive, swim, or climb anything after combining them. Don't add sleep aids, allergy pills, muscle relaxers, or anxiety medicines on top. If you're over 65, have glaucoma, trouble urinating, or a breathing condition, ask a doctor before taking meclizine at all, with or without alcohol.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining meclizine with alcohol if** you take any other medicine that causes drowsiness (sleep aids, opioids, benzodiazepines, muscle relaxers, some antidepressants), you are over 65, you have glaucoma, an enlarged prostate, asthma or COPD, or liver problems, or you take meclizine every day for vertigo. **Call 911 right away if** someone who mixed meclizine and alcohol can't be woken up, is breathing slowly or irregularly, is confused or seeing things, or has a seizure.

## What Meclizine Is (and Why It's Sold Under So Many Names)

Meclizine is an older-style antihistamine. It belongs to the same broad family as Benadryl (diphenhydramine) and original Dramamine (dimenhydrinate), sometimes called first-generation antihistamines. What makes these older drugs different from newer allergy pills like Zyrtec or Claritin is that they cross easily into the brain. That's exactly why they work for motion sickness, and it's also why they make you drowsy.

You'll find meclizine under several names:

- **Bonine:** an over-the-counter chewable tablet, usually 25 mg, popular with cruise passengers.
- **Dramamine Less Drowsy** (and **Dramamine All Day Less Drowsy**): over-the-counter meclizine tablets, usually 25 mg. Note that *original* Dramamine is a different drug, dimenhydrinate. We cover that one in our [Dramamine and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/dramamine-and-alcohol).
- **Antivert** and generic meclizine: prescription versions, often in 12.5 mg, 25 mg, or 50 mg strengths, commonly prescribed for vertigo (a spinning sensation caused by inner ear problems).
- **Store brands:** labeled "motion sickness relief, less drowsy formula" or similar. Check the active ingredient line for "meclizine HCl".

All of them carry the same active ingredient, so the alcohol advice in this article applies to every one.

### How meclizine works

Your sense of balance comes from your inner ear, which sends signals to your brain about movement. When your eyes and inner ear disagree (you're inside a rocking cabin that looks still), your brain gets mixed signals and nausea follows. Meclizine dampens those signals by blocking histamine (H1) receptors and acetylcholine receptors in the pathways between the inner ear and the parts of the brain that trigger nausea and vomiting.

The same blocking action in the brain causes the main side effects: drowsiness, dry mouth, blurred vision, and sometimes mild confusion. Meclizine is known for being *less* sedating than dimenhydrinate or diphenhydramine, which is why it gets the "less drowsy" marketing. But less drowsy is not the same as non-drowsy. Plenty of people still feel noticeably tired on it, especially at 50 mg.

### How long it lasts

Meclizine is a long-acting drug. One dose generally controls motion sickness for about 24 hours, which is why the label tells you to take it once a day, about an hour before you travel. Its half-life (the time it takes your body to clear half of it) is roughly 5 to 6 hours in most adults, according to the prescription label. Your liver breaks it down mainly through an enzyme called CYP2D6. People vary a lot in how active that enzyme is, so some clear meclizine faster and some slower, and that changes how long the drowsiness lasts.

The practical takeaway is simple: **if you took meclizine in the morning, it is still in your system at dinner and at the bar that night.**

## Why Meclizine and Alcohol Don't Mix: Sedation Stacking

Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant. It slows brain activity by boosting the brain's main calming chemical (GABA) and blocking one of its main excitatory chemicals (glutamate). Meclizine slows brain activity a different way, by blocking histamine and acetylcholine, which normally help keep you alert.

Because the two drugs work through different systems, their effects add together. Neither one cancels the other out. Here's what that looks like in real life:

- **More drowsiness.** You may feel much sleepier after one or two drinks than you normally would. Some people describe feeling "hit hard" by a single cocktail.
- **Worse balance and coordination.** Both drugs affect your balance. Together they make stumbling and falls more likely, which matters a lot on a moving ship, a wet pool deck, or stairs.
- **Slower reaction time and poorer judgment.** This is why driving, boating, and swimming are off the table.
- **More dizziness.** This can feel ironic when you took meclizine to stop dizziness, but alcohol itself causes dizziness and the [drunk spins](/never-hungover/drunk-spins), and meclizine won't fully protect you from that.

### Anticholinergic side effects can pile up

Meclizine blocks acetylcholine, which gives it what doctors call anticholinergic side effects: dry mouth, constipation, blurry vision, trouble urinating, and, in some people, confusion. Alcohol doesn't share that mechanism, but it does make you dehydrated and can worsen confusion. In older adults especially, the combination can tip someone into real confusion or a fall. The American Geriatrics Society's Beers Criteria, a widely used list of medicines to use cautiously in people over 65, includes first-generation antihistamines like meclizine for this reason.

### The breathing question

Many people worry about whether this combination can stop your breathing. For a healthy adult taking a normal dose of meclizine and drinking moderately, serious breathing problems are unlikely. Meclizine on its own isn't known as a breathing suppressant at normal doses. The danger rises when you add things that *do* suppress breathing, such as opioid painkillers, benzodiazepines like Xanax or Ativan, or very heavy drinking. That's why the warning box above lists those medicines.

## What the Label and Official Guidance Actually Say

The US Drug Facts label on over-the-counter meclizine products is direct. It tells you to:

- **Avoid alcoholic drinks** while using the product.
- Be aware that **alcohol, sedatives, and tranquilizers may increase drowsiness.**
- **Be careful when driving a motor vehicle or operating machinery.**
- **Ask a doctor before use** if you have glaucoma, a breathing problem such as emphysema or chronic bronchitis, or trouble urinating due to an enlarged prostate.
- **Ask a doctor or pharmacist before use** if you are taking sedatives or tranquilizers.

The prescription label for Antivert adds that meclizine can impair the mental and physical abilities needed for driving and should be used with caution alongside alcohol and other central nervous system depressants, because of the risk of increased drowsiness.

Notice what the label does *not* say. It doesn't claim a single drink is dangerous. It says to avoid alcohol and warns that drowsiness increases. That's a sensible and cautious position, and the main risks it's protecting you from are accidents, falls, and over-sedation rather than organ damage.

### What about the liver?

Unlike acetaminophen (see our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol)), meclizine isn't known for causing liver damage alongside alcohol. The concern with this pair is your brain, your balance, and your safety, not your liver. If you have liver disease, though, ask your doctor about meclizine anyway, because a damaged liver may clear the drug more slowly and make the drowsiness last longer.

## The Cruise and Travel Scenario: Bonine Plus Drinks

This is the situation most people searching "meclizine and alcohol" are in. You're on a cruise, a boat trip, or a long drive. You took Bonine or Dramamine Less Drowsy to stay ahead of motion sickness, and there's a drink package, a beach bar, or a wedding toast ahead of you.

### Why trips make this combination more risky

On a trip, the meclizine-plus-alcohol effect rarely happens in isolation. Several things stack on top of each other:

- **A moving surface.** Balance problems that are a minor issue on land become a fall risk on a rolling deck, slick stairs, or a tender boat.
- **Sun and heat.** Dehydration makes both dizziness and hangovers worse. Meclizine's dry-mouth effect can hide how thirsty you actually are.
- **Long drinking windows.** Drink packages encourage sipping from lunch until late, which means more total alcohol overlapping with a drug that lasts all day.
- **Water nearby.** Pools, hot tubs, snorkeling, and beach swimming after drinking are risky on their own. Adding a sedating drug makes them more so.
- **Other medicines in the bag.** People often pack a sleep aid for the flight, an allergy pill, or a pain reliever. Several of those also cause drowsiness.

For a fuller set of cruise-specific tips, see our guide to [drinking on a cruise](/never-hungover/drinking-on-a-cruise).

### Does alcohol make seasickness worse?

It can. Alcohol affects the fluid in your inner ear and your brain's balance processing, which is one reason you get the spins when drunk. Alcohol also irritates the stomach and causes dehydration. So drinking heavily on a rough sea day can make motion sickness worse even if you've taken meclizine. And if you end up vomiting from alcohol, that's not something meclizine is designed to fix.

### Smarter ways to drink if you get seasick

If you want to enjoy a drink or two without feeling wrecked, these habits help:

1. **Take meclizine early.** The label suggests one hour before travel. Taking it in the morning rather than late afternoon means less of the peak effect overlaps with evening drinks.
2. **Use the lowest dose that works.** Many people do fine on 25 mg. Talk to a pharmacist before going above that, especially if you plan to drink.
3. **Eat first.** Food slows alcohol absorption and settles your stomach.
4. **Cap it at one or two drinks.** Alternate every drink with a full glass of water.
5. **Choose lighter drinks.** Beer or wine spritzers rather than frozen cocktails with multiple shots.
6. **Skip the sleep aid.** Don't add diphenhydramine (Benadryl, ZzzQuil), doxylamine (Unisom), or melatonin-plus-antihistamine combos on top.
7. **Stay away from water and heights after drinking.** No hot tub, no pool, no leaning on the rail.
8. **Have a buddy.** Someone who knows you took a motion sickness pill and can keep an eye on you.

## How Long to Wait: Timing Meclizine and Alcohol

There's no official waiting period, but you can make sensible choices based on how the two drugs behave.

### How long after taking meclizine can you drink?

Because meclizine works for about 24 hours, any drink on the same day overlaps with it. The strongest drowsiness tends to be in the first several hours after a dose. If you took it in the morning, an evening drink will overlap with less of the drug than a drink at lunch, but there's still some in your system. Treat the whole day as a "go easy" day.

### How long after drinking can you take meclizine?

Your body clears alcohol at roughly one standard drink per hour for many people, though this varies with weight, sex, food, and genetics. Our guide on [how long alcohol stays in your system](/never-hungover/how-long-does-alcohol-stay-in-your-system) explains the details. After a light night, waiting until the alcohol has cleared before taking meclizine is reasonable. After a heavy night, wait until the next morning and make sure you're steady on your feet before taking it.

## Meclizine for Vertigo: Daily Use and Alcohol

Some people take meclizine regularly, prescribed by a doctor for vertigo, Ménière's disease, or other inner ear problems. If that's you, the advice changes a little:

- **Daily use means constant overlap.** If you take it every day, every drink you have overlaps with it. Ask your doctor directly how much alcohol, if any, is reasonable for you.
- **Alcohol can trigger some kinds of vertigo.** For people with Ménière's disease, many doctors advise limiting alcohol, along with salt and caffeine, because it may affect the fluid balance in the inner ear.
- **Vertigo plus alcohol plus a sedating drug is a fall risk.** This matters most for older adults, who are more likely to be prescribed meclizine for dizziness in the first place.

If you notice your vertigo gets worse after drinking, mention it to your doctor. It may be a sign your inner ear is sensitive to alcohol.

## Can You Take Meclizine for a Hangover?

Some people reach for meclizine the morning after because it helps with nausea and dizziness, two classic hangover symptoms. Here's the honest picture:

- **It may help the queasy, spinning feeling.** Meclizine is an anti-nausea drug, and hangover nausea is partly driven by the same brain areas it targets.
- **It may make the tiredness worse.** Hangovers already leave you foggy and drained. Adding a sedating antihistamine can make the day feel longer.
- **Only take it once the alcohol has cleared.** If you're still drunk or might be, wait.
- **It doesn't address the cause.** Meclizine does nothing for dehydration, low blood sugar, poor sleep, or the inflammation that drives hangover symptoms.

For other ways to settle a hangover stomach, our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) covers food, fluids, and over-the-counter options. If you're comparing anti-nausea medicines, our [Zofran and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/zofran-and-alcohol) explains a prescription option that works differently.

**When not to self-treat:** if you're vomiting repeatedly, can't keep water down for several hours, see blood in your vomit, or feel confused, see a doctor. That's not a hangover to manage with a motion sickness pill.

## Meclizine vs Other Motion Sickness Options When You Drink

If you know you'll be drinking on a trip, it's worth knowing the alternatives. None of these are "alcohol-safe," but they differ in how much drowsiness they add.

| Option | Main ingredient | Drowsiness | Alcohol warning |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bonine, Dramamine Less Drowsy | Meclizine | Mild to moderate | Yes, avoid alcohol |
| Original Dramamine | Dimenhydrinate | Moderate to strong | Yes, avoid alcohol |
| Benadryl | Diphenhydramine | Strong | Yes, avoid alcohol |
| Scopolamine patch (prescription) | Scopolamine | Mild to moderate, plus dry mouth and blurred vision | Yes, can increase drowsiness and confusion |
| Ginger | Ginger root | None known | No specific warning |
| Acupressure wristbands | No drug | None | None |

A few notes on these:

- **Original Dramamine** tends to be more sedating than meclizine, so the combined effect with alcohol is usually stronger.
- **Benadryl** is sometimes used for motion sickness, but it's one of the most sedating options. See our [antihistamines and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/antihistamines-and-alcohol) for more on that family of drugs.
- **The scopolamine patch** (Transderm Scop) is a prescription option worn behind the ear. It's also anticholinergic and its labeling warns about alcohol and drowsiness, so it isn't a free pass either.
- **Ginger and wristbands** have mixed evidence. Some people find them helpful for mild motion sickness, and they don't add sedation, so they're worth trying if your symptoms are mild and you plan to drink.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

The meclizine-plus-alcohol combination is a bigger deal for some people than others. Talk to a doctor or pharmacist before mixing them if any of these apply:

- **You're over 65.** Older adults are more sensitive to anticholinergic drugs and more likely to become confused or fall.
- **You take other sedating medicines.** This includes sleep aids, opioids, benzodiazepines, muscle relaxers, gabapentin, some antidepressants, and some antipsychotics. Combining several sedating drugs with alcohol is where serious problems happen.
- **You take medicines that slow meclizine breakdown.** Because meclizine is processed by the CYP2D6 enzyme, drugs that block that enzyme (some antidepressants such as fluoxetine and paroxetine, and bupropion, for example) may make it last longer. Your pharmacist can check your list.
- **You have glaucoma, an enlarged prostate, or trouble urinating.** Meclizine can worsen these, and the label says to ask a doctor first.
- **You have asthma, COPD, or another breathing condition.** The label asks you to check with a doctor first.
- **You're pregnant or breastfeeding.** Ask your doctor before using meclizine. Alcohol is not recommended during pregnancy at all.
- **You're driving, operating a boat, or in charge of children.** Any amount of alcohol on top of meclizine affects the judgment and reaction time you need.

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help

Most of the time, combining meclizine with a drink or two just makes you sleepy and a bit wobbly. Know the signs that it's gone beyond that.

**Call 911 or go to the emergency room if someone who combined meclizine and alcohol:**

- Can't be woken up, or wakes up but can't stay awake
- Is breathing slowly, shallowly, or irregularly
- Is very confused, agitated, or seeing or hearing things that aren't there
- Has a seizure
- Has a very fast heartbeat with hot, dry, flushed skin (signs of too much anticholinergic effect)
- Shows signs of alcohol poisoning, such as vomiting while passed out, cold or bluish skin, or very slow breathing. Our [alcohol poisoning signs guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs) explains what to look for.

If you're not sure whether someone took too much of a medicine, you can call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US) for free, confidential advice at any hour.

**See a doctor soon (not an emergency) if you notice:**

- Dizziness or vertigo that keeps getting worse, or comes back every time you drink
- Trouble urinating after taking meclizine
- Eye pain or sudden blurred vision (possible glaucoma flare)
- Repeated vomiting that won't settle

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

Let's be clear about what a supplement can and can't do here. **There is no good evidence that DHM (dihydromyricetin) reduces the sedation from combining meclizine with alcohol, and it does not make the combination safe.** If you took meclizine, the label warning still applies whatever supplements you take.

Where DHM may fit is the broader goal of feeling better the day after drinking. DHM is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and hangover symptoms. Most of the research is in animals and lab models, with limited human data, so it's promising rather than settled. Some travelers pack it alongside their motion sickness tablets for nights when they do drink. If you want to try it, popular options include [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), a budget-friendly pure DHM tablet, and [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which adds L-cysteine and electrolytes. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing, and our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) explains what's known about DHM alongside common medicines. As always, ask your pharmacist before adding a supplement if you take prescription drugs.

The habits that matter most are still the basic ones: drink less, eat first, alternate with water, and sleep. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) goes through the ones with the best evidence.

## The Bottom Line

Meclizine and alcohol both make you drowsy and unsteady, and together the effect is stronger. That's why every meclizine label, from Bonine to Antivert, tells you to avoid alcohol. For a healthy adult on a single dose, one or two drinks is unlikely to cause serious harm, but it will probably make you more tired and less coordinated than you expect, so skip driving, swimming, and heights. The real danger comes from heavy drinking, high doses, older age, and stacking other sedating medicines on top. If you take meclizine daily or take other medications, ask your pharmacist or doctor what's safe for you.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking meclizine?**

The label for over-the-counter meclizine tells you to avoid alcoholic drinks, because both cause drowsiness and together the effect is stronger. For a healthy adult, a single drink after a standard 25 mg dose is unlikely to be dangerous, but you will probably feel more tired and less steady than usual. Don't drive, swim, or handle anything risky, keep it to one or two drinks at most, and ask a pharmacist or doctor first if you take other sedating medicines or are over 65.

**How long after taking meclizine can I drink?**

There is no official waiting time. Meclizine works for about 24 hours, and its half-life is roughly 5 to 6 hours in most adults, so some of the drug is still in your system the whole day you take it. In practice, plan on any drink that day overlapping with the medicine, and drink less than you normally would. If you want to drink in the evening with less overlap, talk to a pharmacist about taking a lower dose or timing it earlier.

**How long after drinking can I take meclizine?**

A reasonable approach is to wait until the alcohol has cleared, which takes about one hour per standard drink for many people, though it varies. If you had a lot to drink, wait until the next morning and make sure you feel steady before you take it. Taking meclizine while you are still drunk adds sedation on top of sedation.

**Is Bonine the same as meclizine?**

Yes. Bonine is a brand of meclizine sold over the counter, usually as a 25 mg chewable tablet. Dramamine Less Drowsy and Dramamine All Day Less Drowsy also contain meclizine. Antivert is the prescription brand, often used for vertigo. The alcohol warning is the same for all of them because the active ingredient is the same.

**Is meclizine safer with alcohol than regular Dramamine?**

Somewhat, for most people. Meclizine tends to make people less drowsy than dimenhydrinate (original Dramamine), so the combined drowsiness with alcohol is usually milder. It is still a sedating antihistamine, though, and its label still says to avoid alcohol. 'Less drowsy' does not mean 'not drowsy'.

**Can I take meclizine for a hangover?**

Meclizine can ease nausea and dizziness, so some people reach for it the morning after. If the alcohol has fully cleared and you feel steady, a single standard dose is unlikely to cause problems for a healthy adult, but it can make the hangover tiredness worse. Don't take it while still intoxicated, and don't use it to keep drinking. If you are vomiting repeatedly or can't keep fluids down, see a doctor instead.

**Can I drink on a cruise if I take Bonine?**

Many people do, but go easy. Seasickness, sun, dehydration, and an unsteady deck all add to the drowsiness and balance problems that come from mixing meclizine with alcohol. Keep it to a drink or two, alternate with water, eat first, stay away from railings and pools after drinking, and avoid stacking other sedating medicines like sleep aids.

**Does DHM make it safe to mix meclizine and alcohol?**

No. There is no good evidence that DHM reduces the sedation from combining meclizine with alcohol, and you should follow the meclizine label warning regardless of any supplement you take. DHM is studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and hangovers, mostly in animal research with limited human data.
